books.section: Regional Differences in British North America

parts.modelAnswer: New England was settled by families who built compact towns around a church and a common. The Chesapeake was settled mostly by single young men who scattered along the rivers on tobacco plantations.
parts.prompt: Identify one difference between New England and Chesapeake settlement described in the passage.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying one difference from the passage, such as families versus single men, compact towns versus scattered plantations, or religion versus work as the reason for coming.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a difference not in the passage, or a vague answer with no difference identified, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: Tobacco farming needed large tracts of land, and planters wanted frontage on the rivers so they could load their crop onto ships. That pulled settlers apart along the waterways instead of gathering them into towns.
parts.prompt: Explain one reason the Chesapeake developed scattered plantations rather than compact towns.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining a cause, such as tobacco needing large tracts of land or planters wanting river frontage for shipping their crop.
scoring.notEarned: Restating that plantations were scattered, with no reason given, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: Both were English colonies settled by English migrants who brought English law, language, and customs with them. Both also had elected assemblies, and both pushed Native peoples off their land as they grew.
parts.prompt: Explain one similarity between New England and the Chesapeake.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one similarity, such as English origin and law, elected assemblies, or expansion onto Native land.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a similarity with no explanation, or giving a difference instead of a similarity, does not earn the point.

stimulus.text: Two English colonies took shape in the 1600s, and they looked very different. New England was settled by families who came together for religion, and they built compact towns around a church and a common. The Chesapeake was settled mostly by single young men who came to work — more than three-quarters of the 130,000 English migrants to the Chesapeake in the 1600s were indentured servants — and they scattered along the rivers on tobacco plantations. New England's people lived longer and had more children; Chesapeake settlers died young, and nearly half of the servants did not survive their terms.
